title: Preferences for Advisor Agreement and Accuracy
description: Participants estimate dates of twentieth-century events, learn from two anonymous computer-generated advisors, and then choose which advisor to consult. One advisor is centered on the correct answer; the other is centered on the participant's initial estimate.

included: 2 practice-with-advice trials with the original correct Practice advisor
two 15-slot familiarisation blocks, including the original attention-check replacements
attention checks at original global trial indices 16 and 36
immediate termination and failure-record preservation after an incorrect attention check
accuracy-, agreement-, and reflected-control advice generation
initial and final estimates in a persistent participant conversation
excluded: post-study advisor ratings not analysed in the paper
Dots Task and categorical Dates Task experiments
implementation_scope.reason: The text-native experimental procedure, including practice and screening controls, is reconstructed from the exact code commit linked by the paper's S1 supplement. Only visual/motor browser mechanics and unanalysed post-study content remain outside the runtime.

sources.license: Article: CC BY; experiment software and materials: MIT

findings.main_hypothesis: Without objective feedback, participants show no consistent group-level preference between the accurate and agreeing advisors, with substantial individual differences.
With objective feedback, participants strongly prefer the accurate advisor over the agreeing advisor.
Advice reduces date-estimation error more when it comes from the accurate advisor than from the agreeing advisor.
